speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DESIGNATED AREAS-GRANTS TO MANUFACTURING AND PROCESSING ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 19 I made a statement about one of the measures relating to the government's campaign against poverty and inadequate opportunities. I would now like to announce a further measure in this campaign.

This program is designed to encourage the establishment of industry in areas of Canada where there is a special need to raise employment and income and broaden economic opportunity for people. To that end, we are now proposing three major changes in the program that has been in operation under the Department of Industry Act. The present program assists industry in designated areas by certain tax measures; these are of great benefit to companies in a profit position, but are less helpful to new and smaller firms. The Government now proposes to introduce legislation to provide for outright grants to manufacturing and processing enterprises establishing or expanding in designated areas. The grant will be based on the size of the capital investment. It will be 33J per cent on the first $250,000 of investment, 25 per cent on the next $750,000, and 20 per cent on investment above $1 million. The grants will be subject to a maximum of $5 million for any one project, that amount being payable when the investment is $24.6 million or more.
The investment costs to which the grants will be applied are buildings, equipment and machinery, and company expenditures for facilities such as water supplies, where these are company-owned. In addition, if a company has to contribute to the cost of publicly-owned facilities, such expenditures may qualify for the grant. The grants will be available for new projects. They will also be available for the expansion of existing plants, provided the expansion contributes appreciably to improving income and employment opportunities in the area.
The legislation we intend to put before you, to be administered by the Department of Industry, will propose to make the program effective from July 1, and will set a termination date of March 31, 1971. Companies that prefer to take advantage of the existing tax incentives may do so until those incentives expire on March 31, 1967.
The second change that I have to announce in the existing program concerns the inclusion of certain manpower measures. We hope to achieve close co-operation among the firms receiving financial incentives, provincial authorities and the National Employment Service, so that there may be effective planning to meet the long-term manpower needs of the new industries as well as their immediate requirements. The Department of Labour will be ready to assist the provinces in developing new training methods and in other extensions of training programs.
June 7, 1965

The third major change we propose in the policy is an extensive revision and broadening of the areas to which it applies. With this objective we propose to establish new guide lines for the designation of areas where, under the terms of the Department of Industry Act, the industrial incentives will be made available. These guide lines will be the basis for objective standards which will be put in statistical terms by the Governor General in Council.
The purpose of this program is to provide a broad improvement in the incentives to industrial development in those parts of the country were underemployment is most serious. There are many more specific measures that can assist industrial development, and provincial governments are developing such measures in regional development plans within their provinces. As those plans are elaborated it will be this Government's policy to seek the fullest harmonization between its action and provincial programs.
The preparation of this program has already benefited from consultation with provincial governments, who have been made aware of the criteria that we are considering applying to the designation of areas. The application of these criteria would mean that the new program of industrial assistance would be available in almost all of the Atlantic provinces, in substantial areas of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and in considerable areas of Quebec. In the three richest provinces-Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta -some smaller areas would qualify. I cannot go into more detail now because we will not take a final decision about criteria until provincial views have been fully expressed.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, this is one of a series of measures which will be placed before you to combat poverty in Canada. The importance of the present proposals is that Canadians living in areas where jobs are most needed will have a better chance to improve their lives, because of the scope that this program provides for constructive industrial development and improved skills.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one would need more than a few seconds to comment on a measure designed to eliminate poverty in Canada.
However, following the announcement just made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), I should like to make a few remarks.
Canadian industries would certainly be well-advised to take advantage of all measures advocated by both the federal government and the provincial governments. It is to be hoped that they will be interested in the one the Prime Minister announced this afternoon.
The fact that measures are put in the statute books is not enough to help people overcome poverty. Industry must be determined

June 7, 1965
Labour Conditions
to benefit from whatever advantages there are. Often manufacturers are not willing to take advantage thereof because those benefits are only nominal and after you have resorted to some prerogatives of the act, you often find yourself once again in the same alarming position as before, when it is intended, for instance, to reduce unemployment or increase workers' income.
The government must also be commended for having increased the number of designated areas. But this increase should not induce some manufacturers to settle in certain areas of the country for a very limited time and then leave those areas, once they have realized industry is not profitable there. In my opinion it is better in such cases not to take advantage of the benefits of the act if you must let the industry die after a few years, even though a few more people than usual have been employed there.
We must also be glad that the government has decided not to apply this legislation without prior consultation with provinces. The fact that most provinces are interested in this matter indicates that this measure is really very important.
It must be noted, however, that among the wealthiest provinces, that is provinces which have less need for this legislation, are two provinces which adopted Social Credit. One may wonder if it is not really the means to fight poverty without the assistance of the federal government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. Member for Saskatoon (Mrs. Jones) raised a question as to the adequacy of protection to the public in the distribution of the drug trifluoperazine. I have had an opportunity since then to discuss the matter raised with the Director of Food and Drugs and with the Commissioner of Patents.
The drug trifluoperazine is in the nature of a tranquilizer. After the appropriate clinical and other testing, a notice of compliance was granted by the Food and Drug Directorate to the manufacturer in 1958. That manufacturer obtained a patent on the drug in 1961. I am informed that this drug is used by the medical profession not only for hospitalized mental patients, but also as a sedative and tranquilizer. It may only be issued in Canada by prescription. It has been so widely accepted that it now appears as a monograph in the British Pharmacopoeia, which means that it has gained recognition as a standard drug. It should be noted that the hon. Lady has not
June 7, 1965

requested that we limit its distribution or use in Canada.
In March of this year another company applied to the Patent Office for the issue of a licence to manufacture trifluoperazine. On April 23 the applicant company was ordered by the Commissioner of Patents to advertise the application and serve it on the Canadian manufacturer of the drug, the patentee, which was done on the 7th of May.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I am informed that according to the practice of the office of the Commissioner of Patents, a period of 60 days from that date is given to the patentee to oppose the application. This is followed by another 60 days during which the applicant may reply. Therefore, at least until the 7 th of July next the patentee may oppose the application for the licence. Moreover, I am informed that third parties have 30 days from the 15th of June next, that is until the 15th of July, to intervene should they so desire. Therefore, until the 15th of July next, as the earliest possible date, no determination could be made of the licence application and no special order need be given to delay the issue of the licence, as requested by the hon. Lady.
However, the Member for Saskatoon raised a number of points as to procedures which should be followed by the Food and Drug Directorate in dealing with such applications.
Before a new drug may be manufactured and distributed to Canadians, an exhaustive series of clinical and other tests must be completed and the Food and Drug Director's Notice of Compliance issued. This procedure, however, is not required each time a new manufacturer is given the right to produce the same drug. Also, of course, the Food and Drug Directorate ensures that the new manufacturer must comply with our regulations respecting drug manufacture. The hon. Lady has suggested that before such a new manufacturer be allowed to distribute a proven drug, the law should require the whole new drug procedure be reundertaken. My officials can foresee certain difficulties here. Nevertheless, since we all hold foremost the safety of the public, and so as to be as sure as we can that our procedures will result in the highest protection to the Canadian public, I am referring this suggestion to a committee of experts to advise me whether such a procedure is warranted. I would hope that such a report might be in my hands and communicated to the House prior to the 15th of July, the expiry for the intervention of third parties in this licence application.
The hon. Lady raised one other point regarding consultation between the Commis-

subsubtopic: SOUTH VIET NAM-POSSIBILITY OF RECONVENING GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the debates that are taking place at the present time in the United States regarding the ever more serious situation in South Viet Nam, I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether the Government has felt impelled to communicate with the United States, and the other nations comprising membership in the Geneva Conference, with a view to reconvening that conference, or urging that some action be taken in this regard to calm the fears that are widely expressed respecting the situation in Southeast Asia, which holds perils for all mankind?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SOUTH VIET NAM-POSSIBILITY OF RECONVENING GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my right hon. friend's question has been stimulated by the statements made over the week end, with regard to the situation in Viet Nam, by a number of prominent political personalities in the United States.
The Government shares the concern which all responsible bodies feel about the situation in Viet Nam. The Government has lost, and continues to lose, no opportunity of exercising whatever influence it possibly can in trying to bring about a ceasefire.
I may say that on May 31 the representative of Canada on the International Supervisory Commission was authorized to proceed to Hanoi and made a contact there with the foreign minister of the government of North Viet Nam in order to indicate the concern which the people of Canada feel with regard to developments in Indochina.
He wanted to ascertain as well, as a spokesman for the Canadian Government, the reaction of the North Vietnamese Government to the interruption that occurred a few days ago in the bombing by the forces under the command of the United States. The Foreign
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
DEBATES	June 7, 1965
Minister of North Viet Nam indicated that there were four conditions which stood in the way of the negotiations which had been urged on the North by the President of the United States, and which had previously been given support by other countries, including Canada.
I regret to say that the reaction of the North, of Communist China and of other interested countries is such at the moment that these overtures for peace discussions have not won their support. We shall continue to resort to every method known to us to try and gather support for our objectives.
The Government of the United States has said it is prepared to attend a conference on Cambodia without relating that conference to any other question but the dispute on borders between Viet Nam and Cambodia. I would hope that this position may yet encourage all concerned to have a conference on Cambodia with, I would think, quite possibly useful results.

subsubtopic: SOUTH VIET NAM-POSSIBILITY OF RECONVENING GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Minister say what are the four elements on which Hanoi seems to be insisting? Does he not agree that the reported statements made by Mao in Tanzania yesterday were of such an inflammatory nature as to indicate that so far as Communist China is concerned, and under it Hanoi, at the moment there is not much hope of the achievement of the objective that all of us have in mind, and which has been accepted in such generous measure by the President of the United States?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SOUTH VIET NAM-POSSIBILITY OF RECONVENING GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The answer to that is, yes. There is no indication, certainly from what Premier Chou En Lai said yesterday in Tanzania, which would warrant a belief that China is disposed not to support the position taken by North Viet Nam.
I regret I do not recall the exact terms of the four conditions, but two of them were that the Government of South Viet Nam and the Government of the United States must deal with the Viet Cong, and that the Government of the United States should withdraw its forces before the talks began.

Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet I should like to reply to a related question asked on May 20 by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie).
That hon. Member asked whether my Department had received any complaints from trade union officials, concerning false information about employment opportunities in British Columbia being given out in the United Kingdom by officers of my Department. I stated at that time that I had received a letter from a trade union official, enclosing a clipping from a newspaper, and I assured the hon. Member that I would look into the matter and reply to his question at an early date. I have now had an opportunity of going into the matter more closely.
On May 15 a Vancouver newspaper quoted the President of Local 452 of the Carpenters Union of Vancouver, stating there is no shortage of skilled workers in British Columbia. On May 13, the Secretary of the same Local wrote me, expressing similar views. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I was and still am puzzled by the views expressed on May 13, by the officials of the union, because of contrary views expressed by Mr. Robert Strachan, M.L.A., the Leader of the N.D.P. in B.C. and the Leader of Her Majesty's Opposition in the B.C. Legislature. Incidentally, Mr. Strachan is a member in good standing of the Carpenters Union.
Mr. Strachan is quoted in a Vancouver newspaper of May 6 as giving a warning that the shortage of skilled labour in British Columbia was skyrocketing. In the same article he went on to say that the construction industry was having a period similar to that of 1956 and 1957 when, due to a shortage of skilled help, companies found themselves having to pay extra overtime costs to attract manpower to their projects. In the same article, Mr. Strachan stated that the cost of
Inquiries of the Ministry schools, hospitals, highways and other public projects in B.C. also were skyrocketing because of lack of skilled workers.
In the course of the inquiries that I have caused to be conducted recently, my Department has been in touch with the Secretary-Treasurer of the Nanaimo-Alberni District Labour Council who, by the way, is the representative in Nanaimo of the Carpenters Union to which I have referred. He confirmed that Mr. Strachan is a member in good standing of that union and, when my Department communicated with him, he asked if my Department had available any immigrant carpenters. He stated that he needed them badly, preferably some from the old country. He said, in fact, that they needed carpenters so badly they would take them into the union at a reduced fee of $25 rather than the normal fee of $100, if we had any available.
In the circumstances, this matter is being very carefully looked into, and I can assure the House that my Department plans no action which will cause hardship to skilled workers in British Columbia. Mr. Speaker, I think that the question before the House is important enough and has such far reaching implications that I do not have to apologize for speaking on this new amendment. I think that the method of approach to this problem is one that I cannot reiterate to the House too often. I do have a feeling that the Government has not given sufficiently serious consideration to realize what this change does to the rights of ordinary Members. I do not believe most Members in this House are aware of the fact that this is a method of closure and that this method of closure proposed by the Government is a most dangerous one. I feel the amendment put forward by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) suggesting 60 per cent is such a change from the usual majority rule that this might help bring to the attention of hon. Members the importance that should be attached to proposed rule change.
Certainly the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn), speaking as a Liberal backbencher, suggested an approach to this problem which, if all his colleagues would look at it, would help everyone understand the problem. I should like to draw to the attention

of the House the reasoning of that hon. Member because it gives an illustration of the dilemma being faced by the Members of this House who feel that Parliament is being criticized and that more efficiency should be brought about in some way. They feel Parliament has a bad image in the country and, more or less without thinking, they have acquiesced in the Government's suggestion that what we need is a change in rules. The last time I spoke on this matter I pointed out that there are many other factors which can have an influence on Parliament, and there are many ways in which Parliament could run more efficiently if people made better use of the rules that now exist.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I should like to point out a few of the things which were said by the hon. Member for St. Paul's in his speech on this subject on June 1 and I will quote three or four passages from his speech that illustrate the dilemma in which many Members of the House find themselves. As recorded near the top of page 1834 of Hansard, the hon. Member said:
-members on this side of the House should insist upon the procedural rules being such as to guarantee and entrench the rights of private Members to speak during a debate, while at the same time permitting the debate to be restricted within reasonable limits.
He made it very clear that he wanted the rules to guarantee and entrench the rights of private Members to speak and yet restrict debate. It would be very interesting if the hon. Member were to show how this could be done.
At about the middle of page 1835 the hon. Member was reported as saying:
-though debate may be limited in appropriate cases, there would at the same time be an absolute guarantee that a private Member who wishes to speak on behalf of his constituents cannot in any circumstances be prevented from doing so.
Again he emphasized that though debate might be limited the important thing was the right of a Member to speak on behalf of his constituents and he said this is such an important right for a backbencher that it cannot be interfered with in any circumstances. Again, as recorded at page 1836, the hon. Member expressed a similar feeling when he said:
As a practical matter, all I suggest is that the rules should guarantee the right of a private Member to speak. If that is done, we will continue to do what has been done since there has been a Parliament; we will continue to work out on a sensible, practical basis, speaking orders. As long as that right is guaranteed we will know that we can work out these arrangements in a mutually
June 7, 1965	COMMONS
satisfactory manner. If that right is removed, then it seems to me a fundamental privilege of our constituents is being attacked.
These three quotations from the speech of a Government backbencher, who says he is in favour of the proposed rule changes, indicate exactly the position in which we find ourselves. In winding up his speech what he in effect says is that the important thing is that the right of the private Member cannot be interfered with and that so long as he is given the right to speak it will be possible for us to work out, "in a mutually satisfactory manner", arrangements for everyone to talk. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising today I want to say immediately that I most definitely support the amendment. The amendment asks that there be at least the support of 60 per cent of the Members of this House. In spite of the fact that personally I may believe this is not necessary, having regard to the action the Government has been taking and the attitude they are showing very clearly I support it most wholeheartedly. I referred, Mr. Speaker, to the attitude the Government has been taking. I was not in the House last week due to a rather dubious sort of illness, but I did get around to reading Friday's Hansard, the amendment in particular and also some of the interjections which showed very clearly that Government supporters were not in favour of the amendment.
I wonder why Government supporters would not be in favour of such an amendment? To my mind it demonstrates the fact that probably there is, as usual, still a bit of arrogance on the part of the Government and its supporters. They fail to realize that when they sneer at and interrupt Members on this side of the chamber they are not doing that to a mere individual but to people who represent thousands and even millions of Canadian citizens. When this is done it brings into this Chamber a time-consuming element. I have only to refer to Friday's Hansard to give an example of the amount of time consumed in this Chamber by interjections from the opposite side.
I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that these interjections, uncalled for references, catcalls, or whatever else you would like to call them, are not only time-consuming but are made to people sent here to represent the citizens of this country regardless of party and to fulfil a very real duty, to say the least. Their duty is to represent their constituents in the House in every way possible. How can this be done when there is any form of closure, guillotine, or whatever else you want to call it, used against even the lowliest backbencher, if I may use that term. If there is a limit to the

time allowed for debate in the House, Members cannot fully represent their constituents.
I am not going to deal with this matter at any length whatsoever but in some research in the time available to me I found that history shows that during periods of time with the least restraint on debate, legislation has been passed much more easily and much more rapidly than during times when there was restraint. This may seem at first examination to be somewhat ambiguous but history shows this to be a fact. I can properly appreciate this, I think, because if there is no limitation on debate the points raised, whether in opposition or in support of a measure, can be fully dealt with, explained and answered and therefore the debate may well come quickly to an end. But when there is any sort of limitation it seems to me that you set up some sort of resistance and when you do that you have, bluntly speaking, a fight on your hands.
We have an example of this every day. Consider the question period in the House. Questions have been avoided, sidestepped and taken as notice. All the way up and down the line Government ministers are trying to sidestep issues. They are taking too much time. A great many questions are still unanswered, although last week a great number were put on the order paper.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Yet the Government and its supporters blame the Opposition for taking the time of the House to the extent that they now want to alter the rules. As the hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) so ably pointed out-I was amazed by the statistics he put on the record-when the previous Government had the greatest majority ever known in the House only 15 per cent of the time spent in this Chamber was taken by the Government and its supporters. The result was more legislation passed during that period of time than any comparable period in Canadian history. That is a very real example of free debate. Certainly there was no suggestion of any form of closure or guillotine, or whatever you want to call it.
I was also reminded by the hon. Member's speech of the part played by the private Member and backbencher in the House. I fully realize the position we are in. I do not try to monopolize the time of the House, as you know, Mr. Speaker, although there are times when I must speak, particularly on matters relating to the support of those in

my constituency and more particularly on matters concerning the nation as a whole.
I am also reminded, having done a little research, that the essence of the motion before us is to cut off the opportunities to speak of the backbenchers in this Chamber, which I believe very strongly is grievously wrong. I would re-emphasize that I hope the Government-I hope the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) is listening-will reconsider any form of limitation of debate.
Another and historical point I might make relates to the fact that the British parliamentary system has doubtless been the most successful democratic system the world has ever known for almost 700 years. Therefore we should be very careful before changing any rules, particularly those relating to limitation of debate. I am a backbencher, one of the lowliest, but if my time is limited or if debate in the Chamber is limited to the point where I have no opportunity to speak then it does not really save the time of the House and it does affect me seriously as a Member. What the motion is doing is depriving thousands, in some cases tens of thousands, of people of representation under a so-called democratic form of Government.
I doubt very much that anyone in this Chamber can really condone that sort of motion. This is the real essence of this matter. Regardless of party, any time that any Member of the House is cut off it is my opinion that much more than time is cut off; the very essence of democracy is cut off.
I should like to give some examples of time wastage in the House and I should like to put them on record while speaking to this amendment. The only reason the amendment has been moved and is before us today is that it is necessary. This motion has been moved by the Government to save the time of the House. If the Government is as sincere as it says it is-in my opinion its actions speak louder than its words-then why was it necessary to take up so much time over the famous budget? That was no fault of the Opposition or of the other Opposition parties in this Chamber. Yet the budget took up much time. It would take a great deal of time to quote from Hansard the points made by many Members of the House, not only Members of the Opposition, but before the rules are changed I might even be allowed to do that.

We in this House have found it necessary to debate the proposed changes to our rules and relate them to particular incidents which have happened in the recent past. I do not take pleasure in rehashing these incidents but, as I said earlier their discussion has consumed a great deal of time in this Chamber. I suggest that the consumption of time, particularly in relation to these incidents, is a direct result of Government action. I should like to ask those individuals occupying the front benches on the other side of the House, particularly the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith), whether It is the Government's intention that the Opposition shall no longer have the opportunity to debate important issues such as the Banks case and, more recently, the Rivard case. The main point I have in mind at this time is one which other hon. Members as well as members of the press have tried to impress upon the Government. It is that every Member of the House, no matter to which party he or she belongs, should have freedom of speech and the opportunity to debate important issues in the House. By adopting the proposed Government measure now before us we will be doing nothing to protect that right. It will on the contrary, diminish that right and in fact whittle away democracy itself.

I should like to conclude my remarks on this point by suggesting to the President of the Privy Council, the Government and its supporters, as well as all Members of all other Parties in the House, that they should consider the consequences of the proposal now before us before allowing it to pass. Mr. Speaker, I intend to confine my remarks on the subject of this debate to two points, the limitation of time and the restriction on individual Members of Parliament. May I say at the outset that the speeches I have heard and read from the commencement of this debate have been extremely sincere and have indicated there is a general feeling that, although some changes should be made, nothing so drastic as proposed by the Government should be accepted.
It is my feeling that any limitation whatsoever on the time of debate is in fact a limitation on the rights of individual private Members and I am completely opposed to it. If the majority is of the opinion that some changes should be made and some limitations effected, I suggest that this could be accomplished more satisfactorily by adopting the principle of the proposed amendment, namely, that before any limitation can be applied 60 per cent of the Members present in the House must vote in favour of such a limitation.
I should like to direct my remarks first to some comments about rule changes made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) during his original speech on this resolution. That right hon. gentleman said:

In one sense it is domestic housekeeping, the amendment of our own rules, and it is being put forward as domestic housekeeping in no partisan way, because every Member of the House, whatever party he may represent, has his own interest in the rules of the House and its procedures.
I agree wholeheartedly with that part of his statement. In commenting about the changes to be made he suggested that this is a departure in the conduct of parliamentary business and therefore in the operation of democracy itself. I agree with that statement. Later on he says:
If they are put into effect I believe they will reconcile or go some way toward reconciling the right of discussion with the right of decision.
We agree to some extent in this regard, and feel that there is merit in that suggestion. We also agree with the suggestions in relation to committee discussions. However, in regard to the limitation on private Members in any debate I totally disagree. May I call it five o'clock.

of the House in relation to the asking of questions is a departure from every established principle of which I have ever heard governing parliamentary debate.

I believe it is a very healthy thing whenever there is a shadow of doubt concerning a Civil Service competition to place questions on the order paper. Who were the successful applicants and in what order were they placed? I have found this invaluable in every case that has been brought to my attention. Many misconceptions apply in these circumstances. There is no substitute for setting out the outcome in the public record. It is the healthy and democratic thing to do. If there is any question whatever of concealment of the facts or concealment of information, simply put a question on the order paper and get the record for all to see.
We have seen, Mr. Speaker, an extension of questions and have observed a very great extension of the questions by some hon. Members. I venture to suggest that these questions are actually drawn up by research people who are looking into one matter or another and they are placed on the order paper in the name of one Member or another. I have seen a large number of really technical questions about various forms of research, drugs, and so on. We had a Hansard Index which was reproduced in a riding and right at the top the question was asked, who works for you? The Member, who had had a lot of references and who had devised questions for the order paper, had his name mentioned in the Index each time a return was made. Evidently this was the way you were to judge whether or not such a Member was effective. This suggests a complete reversal of the purposes for which we were elected. We were not elected to act as intermediaries whereby a great many technical, research questions could be placed under our names on the order paper, with their number being a measure of our performance.
There is no question but that the rules are quite clear. If you turn to citation 171 of Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, you will find

the rules which generally govern this matter. We learn that in putting a question a Member must confine himself to the narrowest limits; that observations which might lead to debate cannot be regarded as, coming within the proper limits of a question; that the purpose of a question is to obtain information and not to supply it to the House. There are something like three pages of comment which state that questions cannot be ironical, rhetorical, offensive, trivial, vague or meaningless, repeat in substance a question already answered, inquire whether statements made in a newspaper are true or contain an expression of opinion. The rules are clear. I suggest it is equally clear that the rules have not always been applied with the strict impartiality which would be in the best interests of this House in putting questions on the order paper. I note a question on the order paper, for example, which asks, when will this session of Parliament end? It was a question put formally in writing on the order paper. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) was just concluding his remarks and I gathered from the comments of some of my colleagues that I had been implicated and charged with having improper access to documents, and so on and so on. Under the strict rules of privilege I should have replied then and there. I did not understand the remarks which had been made, but when I read Hansard I was shocked and hoped that the hon. Member for Port Arthur would take the opportunity to correct Hansard because several of the statements he made were obviously foolish and totally indefensible. I regret that to date he has not seen fit to do so.
[Mr. Francis.)
I sent him notice of when this notice of motion was coming up and I had believed he would be here today to reply to the remarks which I am making. Having missed the opportunity to raise this matter at the earliest possible time on a question of privilege, I am taking advantage of this notice of motion to answer some of the charges made on that occasion.
There is first the question about second class Members of Parliament. It is said of those on the Government side, "You are now a second class Member of Parliament and have not the same privilege to ask questions as does the Opposition". This is totally fallacious, malicious and misleading and without a shred of evidence to support it, as is the suggestion that somehow there is something irregular in Members on the Government side trying to probe or get access to information.
In the short period of time, in excess of two years, in which I have been a Member of the House I have observed with great interest the way in which some Members have managed to place well informed and highly intelligent questions on the order paper, including the hon. Member for Port Arthur on a number of occasions. Access to information is always a ticklish business. I was a civil servant for some nine years, Mr. Speaker. I know the rules that govern Civil Service behavior and I was careful to observe them to the best of my competence when I was a civil servant. But it is quite clear that some Members do manage to get access to information.
I remember the McIntosh letter, a photostat of which the hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) waved in the House. It is an interesting point how he had access to get a photostatic copy of a highly confidential letter. There have been many other instances but, Mr. Speaker, I think we have to say that the relationship between a Member of Parliament and his source of information is to a considerable degree a privileged relationship.
I deny flatly and categorically that I had access to Department of Justice files when framing a question which was placed on the order paper. I deny that without any reservation, and had the matter been made one of a charge which would have gone to the Committee on Privileges and Elections-that is where it should have gone-I could have set the record clear before that committee. However, it did not take that form. It did not go before that committee. It was taken under
June 7, 1965

advisement by the Speaker who found, to all intents and purposes, that he could detect nothing irregular. But it leaves an unpleasant taste in Parliament. It leaves an innuendo on the record and it is not in the interests of Members to do this.
I have looked into the question of the relationship of civil servants to Members of Parliament. Usually in many cases it is members of the Civil Service who are the most informed parties, who are the people in a position to give clues or hints and to drop suggestions for further investigation. I find that according to Beauchesne there is a very serious doubt whether a civil servant is doing any wrong in many cases in passing information to a Member of Parliament.
Beauchesne, in an appendix to the fourth edition, deals with the report of a select committee appointed by the United Kingdom House of Commons to inquire into the applicability of the Official Secrets Acts to members of the House. This was a committee established in 1939 and its findings are very interesting. I quote from the official report of the committee as found in the appendix to Beauchesne, page 417:
Whether the person to whom the defendant communicated the information, though not a person to whom he was authorized to communicate it, was yet a person to whom it was in the interest of the state his duty to communicate it would be a question for the jury to determine. The executive would not have the final word on the question. A measure of protection is thus afforded to any person who communicates information to a Member of Parliament.
In other words, as I read Beauchesne an employee of the Crown in possession of information who communicates that information to a Member of Parliament is in something of a privileged position should he be charged with a violation, and the charge could not simply be determined by the executive branch of the Government. There would clearly be a right to a jury trial and there would be certain privileges which could be invoked by a civil servant contending it was in the public interest to disclose that information to a Member of Parliament.
This kind of thing goes away back into the privileges of Members, back to time immemorial. I have listened, as have many other Members, to the debate which preceded this one and the allegations of restrictions on private Members and the alleged usurping of authority by the executive at the expense of the legislative branch. But the proposition that a Member of this House has not the right to probe, to ask questions, to place
Written Questions
questions on the order paper for answers that he feels it is proper to get, together with the suggestion that if a civil servant communicates with a Member of Parliament this would somehow be improper collusion and the suggestion that Members on this side of the House on the Government backbenches should be restricted or denied the same opportunities as Members on the other side, is a totally preposterous and indefensible proposition and one which should not be treated tolerantly by Members of the House.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that hon. Members will give consideration to supporting this resolution. The result of its adoption would be the establishment of a committee which would take a fresh look at the rules. Maybe the rules are all right. As I read them they sound pretty good, but certainly something is wrong because the questions that are getting on the order paper do not, by my elementary, lay reading of the rules, appear to be consistent with the rules. Perhaps all we have to do is apply the rules more rigorously than has been the case in recent months in which case there would be fewer questions on the order paper. I would also like to think that the procedure of a Member of Parliament, or people representing such a Member on his behalf, taking the Hansard indexes, the overwhelming majority of which refer to questions, and implying that the number of questions shown opposite an hon. Member's name is the measure by which to judge his effectiveness, would cease to be a practice observed by many Members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. Member for Carleton (Mr. Francis), having been stimulated by the hon. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), put this notice of motion on the order paper and has quite properly noted that the hon. Member for Port Arthur is not in his seat. I rise on behalf of the Member for Port Arthur simply to point out that I received a message from his office two or three hours ago that Air Canada was fogbound at the Lakehead last night and as a result he has not been able to get back. He knew this motion was coming up today and had hoped to be here to speak to it.
Obviously it is not necessary for me to defend the hon. Member for Port Arthur. He is very capable of speaking for himself. However, since I have taken the floor there are a few words I should like to say in response to what the hon. Member for Carle-

June 7, 1965
Written Questions
ton has suggested. I do not quarrel with him over the obvious tact that the hon. Member does not really want what his notice of motion asks for, namely, a revision of Standing Order 39(1). What he really wants is a chance to have discussed, in a committee, the whole question which the hon. Member for Port Arthur raised. I see nothing wrong with his wanting that done and I hope the House may let this motion pass so that even if a revision of 39(1) were not to be the result there would be a chance to go into the questions which were raised on March 4 by my hon. friend from Port Arthur. There might, of course, be some problem about the committee's terms of reference but I do not think this would be serious because a committee set up to study 39(1), as suggested by the hon. Member for Carleton, could easily I suppose, consider examples of its use or alleged abuse in recent months.
e (5:20 p.m.)
I am a little concerned about the proliferation of committees on questions of procedure. We are debating at some length-and I say this very mildly without trying to be provocative-a motion of the Prime Minister which includes provision for the setting up of a committee to work out certain rules of procedure in a limited area. Now the hon. Member for Carleton proposes that a committee should be set up to inquire into another aspect of our rules. Some of us think it unfortunate that the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization which met for two years was not re-established this session. Despite everything I am prepared to say in defence of the changes which are now proposed by the Government, I still think we were doing it in a better way, even though it seemed to be taking considerable time. But I hope we shall not set up one committee after another to deal with points of procedure. Taking the motion put forward by the hon. Member for Carleton at its face value, we should be logical and re-establish the Committee on Procedure and Organization to deal with the matter in his motion as well as a number of our rules. I recognize -and I am relying on my memory of what the hon. Member for Port Arthur said about this issue-that my hon. friend gave the hon. Member for Carleton the feeling he had to make the kind of speech which he made today, defending his position as one whose rights are equal to the rights of those who sit on this side of the House. But one of the things which concerns me about the questions which were put on the order paper

by the hon. Member for Carleton and by one or two other Members is that they seemed to violate the rule that questions should seek information, not give it. It occurs to me that this is what was offensive about these questions. They asked whether such and such was true, and the such and such was spelled out in such detail that the answer was given by the very form of the question. However, this was dealt with at some length by the hon. Member for Port Arthur.

speechtext: Would the hon. Member permit a question? I should like to ask the hon. Member through you, Sir, to tell me this: If the question was improper, should it not simply have been rejected? The question having been accepted, was not the proper thing to do to complain about whether the rules were being enforced rather than to make charges against myself?

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER WRITTEN QUESTIONS

That, of course, is the whole issue between the hon. Member for Carleton and the hon. Member for Port Arthur, the issue which the hon. Member for Carleton would like to have discussed by the committee. I think he is perfectly justified in wanting to have it discussed. I did not consult my hon. friend from Port Arthur on this, but I think he would agree that the committee ought to be established so that the whole question might be aired, and he of course would be there to speak for himself.
Perhaps I might say another word about the form of these questions. I recognize that those who have to examine our questions before they are placed on the order paper have a tremendous job to do. Hundreds of questions are given to them. Many of us try to get information by drafting questions which seem to give information. I have had the experience of being told that my questions went too far in this direction. I do not think this is a point on which we should appear to be criticizing the officers who examine or vet these questions. The hon. Member is right. What is needed is not a revision of the rule. Indeed, I think it stands up fairly well. What is needed is a fresh look at it so that all of us, those who draft questions, those who answer them and those who are responsible for them in any way, will pay greater attention to the observance of the rule as it is.
I regret that fog around the Lakehead prevented the hon. Member for Port Arthur from getting here for this debate, and precisely because he is not here I hope the House
June 7, 1965

will let this motion pass so that this matter may go before a special committee and thus be further examined.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER WRITTEN QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The notice of motion placed on the order paper by the hon. Member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) calls for the setting up of a special committee of not more than 15 Members to prepare a revision of standing order 39(1) dealing with the form and content of written questions on the order paper.
It seems to me that in the course of his remarks the hon. Member indicated that what prompted him to put this question on the order paper was the charge of collusion by the hon. Member for Port Arthur involving backbenchers of the Liberal party and Ministers. I think the hon. Member is a little over-sensitive about this particular incident. I was in the House when the alleged charge was made respecting this matter. I will not say a great deal about it because there was some evidence that it might have happened. Yet if one were to be broadminded and give the backbenchers of the Liberal party full credit for asking probing questions to get this kind of information, there would not necessarily have had to be collusion at all.
However, there are some problems respecting 39(1) which need to be looked into so far as I am concerned. If we look at the commentaries respecting 39(1) and citation 171 of Beauchesne to which the hon. Member for Carleton referred a number of times we shall find there are no less than 40 prohibitions stated on page 147 with application to the framing of questions which may properly be placed on the order paper. I agree to a large extent with the hon. Member for Carleton when he said that if all these prohibitions were invoked nothing more would be necessary to prevent the abuses which have become prevalent respecting questions placed on the order paper. But to say these provisions should be applied to every question sent to the officials of this House would be to oversimplify the problem. It is difficult to apply all these prohibitions to some of the questions put forward. It becomes a matter for discretion. Moreover, I am sure the Members who advance these questions do not always agree with the decisions taken by those who look them over.
But it seems to me there are sufficient prohibitions already. If there were some measure of agreement as to how these prohibitions could be applied to the questions, we might be able to make better progress. I am in some
Written Questions
agreement with the hon. Member that we ought to do something about applying the rules we now have. Perhaps the setting up of a committee would be the way to do this. The committee in turn could make recommendations about setting up another committee or a board or a group of men and women to look over these questions and determine whether they meet the qualifications necessary before they can be placed on the order paper.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I am not being over-critical of the officers of this House for allowing a certain number of questions to go through because I know it is possible to word questions cleverly in such a way that you get around certain of the prohibitions. But all this does is to result in a situation where a certain amount of discretion has to be used. I do not know whether you want to call this a screening committee or not, Mr. Speaker, but it seems to me there needs to be this additional care taken in looking over the questions before they are put on the order paper.
Another thing that disturbs us is the type of question that has been getting on to the order paper. You can find all kinds of them on the order paper for today. They are simply questions where Members are using this means, this channel, to have somebody else do their research for them, because a great deal of the information being asked for in the questions that appear on the order paper today is already available to the hon. Members concerned if they would use the facilities of the Library of Parliament and make inquiries in other places where this information is readily available to them. By putting the question on the order paper responsibility is transferred to some departmental official to gather all these facts and figures together and present them in the kind of condensed way that the Member requires.
For example, Mr. Speaker, there are two questions on page 37 of today's order paper Nos. 40 and 42, dealing with the matter of capital punishment. Apparently the Member putting these questions on the order paper simply wants to have all these facts and figures available to him respecting how many death sentences have been commuted, how many persons were executed, how many incidents of bungled hangings appear in the records of Canadian executions, and so on. It does seem to me that this is the kind of question that is seeking information which

June 7. 1965
Written Questions
need not necessarily come from the Department because it is already available to Members from other sources. I am not singling out the hon. Member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) because there are dozens more questions that do exactly the same thing, namely, require officials in departments to make long and detailed exercises in research to gather all this information together. I think this is something of a departure from the original intent and purpose of obtaining information by way of a question on the order paper.
There is another point here, Mr. Speaker. Paragraph (c) of citation 171 of Beauchesne says:
A question oral or written must not multiply, with slight variations, a similar question on the same point.
I have seen 20 questions on the order paper that were almost identical, using the same terminology with the exception of one or two words. So this seems to me to be a clear violation of citation 171 (c); yet they have been allowed on the order paper. I do not know whether the people who screen or look over the questions to decide their propriety have taken into consideration all these 40 prohibitions. At the same time I am not sure that they have had any clear directive from the Members of the House recently as to what they should accept.
I should like to impress upon Members of the House that this is perhaps one thing this committee could do, namely, give some instruction to the people involved as to the propriety of accepting questions that only represent transferring the responsibility for research or accepting a multiplicity of questions on really the same point. That is all we want to say on the matter at this time, Mr. Speaker. We generally agree with the hon. Member for Carleton that some additional instructions ought to be given with regard to allowing questions to be placed on the order paper. But so far as any tightening up of the rules respecting oral or written questions is concerned, it seems to me there are enough rules and prohibitions now for the system to be effective if the rules were applied with the kind of discretion with which most Members in this House would agree.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. B. Slewari (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER WRITTEN QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if Standing Order 39, section 5, as proposed by the Government, passes this House, we can assume that more questions will find their way to the

order paper. I need not remind the House that this proposed Standing Order would limit the time to 30 minutes for questions asked when the orders of the day are called. The result would be the Members would turn increasingly to the order paper question for information, possibly for publicity, and perhaps even to annoy the Government from time to time.
I think we have to recognize that the popularity of the order paper question is now well established. In the last session of this Parliament the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) put down a question concerning the number of questions and motions for papers asked in this House since 1867. The Department of the Secretary of State fortunately was in a position to answer that question. The answer appears at page 12883 of Hansard for March 29, 1965. I wish to mention to you, Sir, that there have been only seven occasions prior to the second session of the twenty sixth Parliament when more than 1,000 order paper questions were asked. Back in 1907-08 1,234 questions were put on the order paper; then in 1912-13 and again in 1914 that number 1,000 was exceeded. It happened again during the second world war, in 1943-44; it happened again in 1947, in 1962-63 and in 1963. In 1963, 1,906 questions were put on the order paper.
In the last session of Parliament, the second session of the present Parliament, the alltime record of 1,906 questions was broken and 3,078 questions were put on the order paper. Of that total 2,932 were dealt with. I use the expression "dealt with" rather than "answered" because occasionally Members will withdraw questions or modify them in some way, so that you cannot say strictly that all 2,932 questions were answered. Of these, 315 were starred questions, and 306 of these were dealt with.
I think we can say that the number of questions on the order paper will increase even without the proposed rule change. This is why the motion of the hon. Member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) inevitably must attract our attention. He is proposing a special committee to deal with the form and content of these questions on the order paper.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
To illustrate that the first and second sessions of Parliament were not abnormal and did not suggest a tendency which is not to develop, let me mention that so far in this session, the third session of the twenty sixth
June 7, 1965

Parliament, 673 questions have been put down, with 208 still on the order paper to be answered. Eleven starred questions are on the order paper to be answered. So I think we can say that this session is following the pattern of the last three sessions. I think we have a trend here: The question on the order paper is becoming an important part of the parliamentary operation.
I think all of us must take these questions and answers given to them seriously. There is no doubt on either side of the House but that the Members of the House deserve and have a right to information concerning public business. Naturally, one's attitude as to the alacrity with which this information is brought forth varies according to where one sits in the House. I suspect that the greatest amount of impatience is concentrated in the Members on the front bench opposite. But then it is not confined to them; I am sure there are backbenchers on the Government side of the House who wonder why Ministers do not give answers at once. I am sure that the people who are most patient of all are the Ministers themselves.
This impatience was demonstrated the other day in the House when the hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) brought up this matter in a very quiet and reasonable way. As reported at pages 1348 and 1349 of Hansard he referred to this matter. He was followed up by Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), who referred to the same matter, as reported at pages 1514 and 1515. I think the importance of the question we are debating today can best be underlined by reading a sentence or two of what was said by the right hon. gentleman at that time. On May 20, 1965, he said:
And so on we could go. Questions have been on the order paper since April 5, April 6 and April 7. If the Government want to help the private Member and are so solicitous to see private Members have every assistance, then why are these questions not answered? As far as starred questions are concerned, there is a philosophy developing that they too can be answered whenever the Government feels like it.
In the United Kingdom all questions are answered within three days. Let us establish this practice in order to help the private Members and we will be able to reduce very greatly the number of questions asked on the orders of the day.
The right hon. gentleman is proposing that if our procedures and our practice in regard to order paper questions could be improved, the number of questions asked immediately before turning to the main business of the day, the orders of the day, would be reduced.
Written Questions
As an illustration of how skeptical one must be with regard to one's views on this whole question, and to suggest how difficult would be the problem of this committee if it were established, I want to mention to you, Sir, that the experience of the right hon. gentleman when he was Prime Minister was not entirely dissimilar to that of those who now sit on the other side of the House. For example, if we examine the order paper for May 20 in the years in which the right hon. gentleman was Prime Minister we will find there was a large number of written questions with dates earlier than April 5. For example, on May 20, 1959 we find questions on the order paper dating back as far as January 27, 1959. I just mention this not to imply that the right hon. gentleman is inordinately impatient; I mention it merely to suggest that here we have a complicated procedure, one which, under Governments of various political persuasions, does cause difficulties.
There were two questions on the order paper for May 20, 1959 dated February 4, one dated February 11, three dated February 20, three dated February 24, two dated February 25, and so on. If we turn to the order paper for May 20, 1960, we will find a similar condition, questions dating back to March 17, March 18, April 1, and so on.

I am sure my hon. friends to the right will be surprised at my rising to defend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), but in all fairness should it not be pointed out that in this session there could not be any questions on the order paper dated earlier than April 5 because that is the day the session started? speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext:
Yes, that is quite right. It is quite obvious that questions could not have gone back beyond April 5 this session, but presumably the right hon. gentleman would not have raised the point had he not thought, a certain number of weeks having elapsed, that that number of weeks was too great. When I find questions going back to January when he himself was Prime Minister, I presume my point is made.
Perhaps part of the difficulty in the thinking of the right hon. gentleman concerns some misunderstanding about the difference between the procedure here and at Westminster. Hon. Members will have noted that the right hon. gentleman said that in the

June 7, 1965
Written Questions
United Kingdom all questions are answered within three days. Of course, that is not accurate. At Westminster they are having difficulty also with their questions. They have appointed a select committee on procedure, one of the tasks of which is to look at the "question time".
I have before me an editorial from the Times for April 27, 1965 and I should like to read a few sentences from it:
The statistics put before the Select Committee on Procedure in relation to question time in the Commons are worth studying. They show, among other things, that the number of questions reached for oral answer has steadily declined since 1937, and, on the evidence of the Speaker, now averages between 30 and 40 daily.
The editorial goes on to explain how unsatisfactory the situation must be for the ordinary Member seeking information.
The Select Committee itself reports that they have received evidence of the increase in the number of questions over recent years. They observe that the number of questions standing in the order book for oral answer on a day in March, 1963, was 551, and that on an equivalent day in 1965 the number was 1,149. We know their procedure is very different. They do not have a daily quiz session as we do here. No questions can be put to a Minister without notice, and almost all those notices appear on the order paper. Private notice of questions is extraordinary and rare.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)

speechtext: Supplementaries are without notice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER WRITTEN QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Supplementary questions are asked, indeed, without notice, but even in this regard restrictions are now being proposed.
The point I am making, Sir, is that then-situation in the United Kingdom is really worse than ours as evidenced by their complaint in respect of the kind of question that is here asked on Orders of the Day, the kind of question which the right hon. gentleman asks so assiduously and which the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre asks so regularly. That is, they complain in the U.K. that "Orders of the Day" questions put down on the order paper stay there for weeks. I am sure neither of those two Members of this House would tolerate that situation here for long if they could do anything about it.
It is not sufficient to suggest that Westminster is a bed of roses for the Opposition Members and that here they have a much more difficult time. It has been said that

perhaps the solution to our problem lies in an enforcement of the rules we now have. Very well, let us attempt to do that; however, it is my feeling that this will not provide a complete answer.
There are one or two points I should like to stress. One of our problems here relates to the distinction we make, a distinction which is not made in the United Kingdom, between written questions placed on the order paper and questions asked when orders of the day are called. Questions placed on the order paper, whether starred or not, tend to be regarded here, if you will, as second class questions. They are not given the prominence in the press or in the House given to questions asked on orders of the day. As a consequence of this, some questions that are not strictly in order on occasion get on the order paper and in some cases less care is taken in preparing the answers. If some method could be devised to give greater prominence to those questions and answers, I believe an improvement in our procedure would follow.
I have noticed in dealing with some of these questions that one of the things which causes delay is that hon. Members sometimes fire a blunderbuss rather than a rifle. If one looks at the questions placed on the order paper in the United Kingdom, he will find they are aimed directly at a particular Department or Minister, asking the Minister of Works or the Home Secretary, for example, about such and such or to explain this or that. Here we find questions directed to the Minister of Public Works, for example, or any other official of the Government, to explain such and such. This requires that a great number of agencies be circularized in order to ascertain whether any information is available. One cannot go to one specified Department or one Minister to obtain the information, rather, one has to cover the whole spectrum of all the departments and agencies comprised in a very involved apparatus of Government.
One way Members could speed things up is by directing their questions to particular Ministers and in a sense putting them on the spot so they cannot say if they wished to do so-this is unlikely with the present Government-that other people will be slow in providing answers so I can take my time.
The rules provide that where a question involves several Departments, it may be made an Order for Return. As an example of the type I have in mind I should like to refer
June 7. 1965	COMMONS
to the question that stands on today's order paper as No. 4. If advantage had been taken of the option available under the rules in relation to such questions and a return had been ordered, the hon. gentleman asking this question probably would not get his answer as quickly as he will under the practice which allows this question to continue on the order paper.
It is possible that Governments-not this one-would follow the rule, out of sight, out of mind. For that reason I believe that if an hon. Member really wants an answer to a question, it is better for it to remain on the order paper as a question rather than to be made an order for return. I may be wrong in this regard, and perhaps the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre will correct me. He might even suggest that I am not being prudent by suggesting that questions should not be hidden away. One of the reasons some questions still remain on the order paper is that they have not been made Orders for Returns because-

That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House; and
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders:
1.	(a) That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 30 days of the time of the House

House of Commons Procedures be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of main estimates; interim supply; and supplementary or additional estimates excepting supplementary or additional estimates introduced after the main estimates have been approved, and excepting always the final supplementary or additional estimates;
(b)	That the number of supply motions be reduced from six to four; and
(c)	That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-four members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon these orders, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
2.	That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read
as follows:
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the Committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and, if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting, interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(7)	No motion made by a Minister under Sections (5) and (6) of this Standing Order shall provide for the allocation of a period of time shorter than two days for the second reading, two days for the committee stage, and one day for the third reading of any bill. For the purposes of this section, third reading shall be deemed to have been considered for one day provided the order for third reading is called as the first item under Government Orders

on a Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, and provided it is continued, if necessary, until the normal time of adjournment on any such day; provided that if a representative of each party has not spoken, the hour for the adjournment of the sitting shall be extended until a representative of each party has had an opportunity to speak. Such an order having been called on any Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, it shall have precedence over all other business until the time of adjournment on that day, unless it is disposed of earlier. Under any other circumstances, a total of five hours shall be deemed to be the equivalent of one sitting day.
(8)	During debate on any item of business or stage thereof for which an allocation of time has been made under this Standing Order, if an amendment is proposed which in the opinion of Mr. Speaker materially changes the item of business or stage thereof and which raises any issue for which in the opinion of Mr. Speaker there has not been or otherwise will not be an adequate opportunity for discussion, Mr. Speaker may announce an extension of not more than two days to the allocated period of time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I had made some comments about certain generalities which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) had set forth at the beginning of his speech during the introduction of these rule changes. I had stated my agreement with certain of these generalities, but then only to a certain extent. Continuing with the remarks of the Prime Minister, I may say that I take courage from his academic summation on the essence of democracy. However, I know, as most of us here know, that scholarly learning and parliamentary practice are poles apart. I should like to quote from the Prime Minister's remarks as they appear at page 1475 of Hansard where he states:
The essence of democracy is that the defence and the criticism are equally important. They are together the process by which guidance and warning is given to the direction of our national affairs. The House of Commons is where the primary defence of Government policy must be made, and where the primary attack on Government policy should be made.
Having said that, I felt that he could have gone a step further. He named two facets of this policy and he could well have set forth a third. In other words, he states here that the
Government and the Opposition will fail if the
June 7, 1965

majority-I am using part of his words- rides roughshod over the strong, sincerely held views of a minority. He says, too, it will fail if the Opposition, that is, the minority, uses obstructionist tactics.
As I have said, in my opinion there is a third facet. A Government may, with the best of intention but the poorest of judgment, produce legislation which patently or on examination is shown to be faulty. It may be that the Government tends toward bureaucratic decisions which are reflected in its legislation. In any event, just as has happened over the last few years, over a period of time a Government itself becomes suspect. I do not feel the present Government has recognized its faults. It says, in effect that all of its legislation is good. The third facet, therefore, is that the Government may think itself infallible, that all its legislation is good and that those who oppose it are obstructionists.
Let us suppose, for instance, that at the present time we have such a Government in Canada. What does the imposition of a time limit on debate mean? Once a time limit has been set, what is the result? It gives the colour of right to the autocratic bureaucracy. It allows the Government to wield a big stick. It allows certain threats, which seems an extraordinary thing. A threat was shown to me today which I should like to point out to the Government. I have here a copy of the Toronto Star and on the front page I see a rather fine picture of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith). The subheading under the picture says, "Election Possible". If they only used black print, everything would be all right. I trust that the President of the Privy Council had this interview and that it is not fictitious. I do not believe in those things. I take it that the President of the Privy Council did have this interview and that it was of such importance his picture, plus the red print, appeared.
