speechtext:
I do not believe it is a red herring. I am going to acquaint the House further with the seriousness of what has been said, what has been quoted from the President of the Privy Council. I am glad to see him in his seat. This is a form of blackmail, incidentally. The article is headed in red, "Mc-Ilraith's Warning". I point out that I believe he is the President of the Privy Council. In somewhat heavier red print, a true Liberal colour, I read:
2067
House of Commons Procedures
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Could be forced to an election.
If we have a limitation on debate, if we allow the Government to say to all the Opposition parties, "If you do not comply with what we say we will wield the big stick," then we will be putting the Government into a position where it can say to us, "Look out, we will blackmail you into this." The proof of that is in this newspaper.
The article goes on to say:
Another "flag debate" stretching Parliament's session into a long, hot summer, was predicted this week end by government House Leader George Mcllraith over the government's proposal to streamline House rules.
Conservative Leader John Diefenbaker likened the proposal to change the rules to the Liberal use of closure in the 1956 pipe line debate. The P.C.'s say it could reduce backbenchers to seldom-heard nonentities.
The government proposes to limit debates by having an all-party House business committee allocate talking time on major legislation. If the committee fails to agree, the government could impose its own time limit, under the proposal.
Today, the House has before it an amendment by Tom Bell (P.C., Saint John-Albert), requiring a 60 per cent Commons majority to put a time limit on debates. Under the present rules there is no time limit on debates.
If it is defeated, Mr. Mcllraith suspects ''more amendments from the Conservatives." He said: "The flag technique all over again."...
Mr. Mcllraith told the Star if there were an election it would be because of "circumstances, not choice."
"1 have always taken the view there is no election in the immediate offing. But the situation of a minority government is such that one could always be forced upon us."
The President of the Privy Council went on to say many more things, but the point I wish to stress is that we are talking against limitation of time and we are doing so for definite reasons. Even half way through this debate the President of the Privy Council has indicated exactly what the Liberal Government will do on occasions when it feels its legislation is being blocked in any way, shape or form. This form of blackmail should receive the strongest censure from all hon. Members, particularly all Opposition Members.
I understand from the tiny voices of some Liberal backbenchers that they are not in complete agreement with the Government's proposal. It will be more than interesting to see how they vote. I can tell them this, "Look out, boys; there is a strong chance of each and every one of you being in the Opposition, and at that time don't forget these rules".

If he feels what he has said is anything less than blackmail, then I ask him to remember the flag debate when this House was blackmailed through a long, hot summer to no effect whatever.
By accepting this limitation of time on debate we will make ourselves subject to an autocratic bureaucracy. There is concrete, simple evidence of that written in red, the Liberal colour, and in black and white in today's Star, and I say it will be a black day if this legislation goes through in its present form. It will allow these political autocrats to say, "We are not cutting debate. Oh, no, we are not bringing in closure. We are not using a guillotine, not a bit of it. We are only following the rules of the House." I ask Liberal backbenchers and all Members of the Opposition to wake up. Do not let this thing go through in its present form. Going back to a few words which the Prime Minister used in his initial speech and turning them a little inside out-he did not say this exactly-I say to him that this is a first step in legal tyranny and intolerance the result of which can only be friction and fury on the part of the Opposition. I believe this; otherwise I would not be saying it. We have it in red, black and white in today's Star.

In this debate on time limitation I think it is wise for us to examine some legislation passed in our recent Parliamentary history which bears out what I am saying. An example is the flag debate. In it the Government said "Look, we have got a mandate to bring in a brand new flag." I do not agree with that statement, but the House sweated for 22 days denying that we should have a flag such as was suggested by the Government on a take it or leave it basis when they said: "You take our flag with two blue bars and three maple leaves and if you do not take it, then, by George, you are going to stay here all summer".
We had that threat just as we have a threat by the President of the Privy Council in today's Toronto Star. If we had had limitation of debate during the flag discussion I point out we would not have the proud flag that is flying over the Parliament buildings today. We would have one with two blue bars and three maple leaves-

Let me deal with the pension plan and what would have happened if we had had limitation of debate during discussion of it. The hon. lady would have had that Government in the worst possible mess this country has ever seen, for she denied the practical consensus of actuaries and economists throughout Canada. By George, I want to point out- here I am, using the first name of the President of the Privy Council, which shows how much the article in the Star has affected me- that had the plan gone through in its original form Canada would have suffered in dollars and cents; it would have suffered in its provincial relationships and it would have suffered from a lousy pension plan. I use the word "lousy" because Churchill used it on a number of occasions. It was only because a united Opposition stood to its guns that the Government was forced to retreat and start again. I could think of many other instances but I will not mention them at this time because attention has been called to them by other Members.
I was interested in the way in which the hon. Member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) had to light in the House the other day to put his views forward. They were most telling. This Government has a history of leaping before
June 7, 1965

it looks. We all remember what happened during those 60 days of decision. How they can sit there and smile now, I do not know.
Why does the Opposition press this issue so strongly? It is because two years have shown the present Government to be most fallible. Thus, no matter what measures it puts forward the Opposition must look at them most carefully to save Canada from falling a victim to the Government's stupidity. The Government has proved itself to be accident prone. The proof is to be found in the legislative record. In these circumstances the Opposition has a special duty to look closely at every item of legislation. All the many hours we have spent-I was going to say "wasted" but that is the wrong word-debating Government business in this House have been well spent. Why has there been this strong and persistent Opposition to the Government? It may, of course, be because we are "agin" them. It may be that we are expressing opinions which are strongly voiced in certain areas of Canada. Many matters have come forward. I remember the vicious fights that arose over the 11 per cent sales tax. The Opposition fought and the Government retreated.
We reminded the Government of the promise they had made to increase the old age pension by $10. Leaders of the party opposite backtracked. Then, I suppose, their public relations men told them: You had better pay that $10. And who paid that $10 in the end? Look at your last income tax return. Ask your accountant if there has been an increase in taxes. You will find that you paid it.
The Prime Minister said the Government should be prepared to bring this measure before the House and stand or fall by it. But it appears to me that once again the brass and the grass are too far apart. I quote from the Globe and Mail an article which appeared on April 7, 1965, written by Fraser Robertson. This screed is very pertinent to the present debate. I do not have time to read it all but this is what it says in part:
They may even be correct and hopeful of proving that the Government is foolishly idealistic in a competitive world and in respect to an economy that is as open to world influences as is the Canadian economy. But businessmen should ask themselves how far they have got in recent years by putting before Governments what they believed to be unassailable arguments based upon knowledge and experience.
The article goes on to say they got nowhere. The pension plan and a few other measures are mentioned. When one considers this record

As Chairman of the Flag Committee at that time, Mr. Speaker, you will know that what I am saying is precisely correct. The Government sat silent, the backbenchers hardly making a speech in all that time; in fact they pointed with pride to the fact that they had not made a speech. Then the moment closure was put on they rose and mealymouthed their way through, not saying anything but taking up the time of the House. This is something against which we must guard.
In general-I am just finishing, Mr. Speaker-and coming back to the Prime Minister's statement that such a change would not be a departure from the function of democracy as it is and that it would go some way toward reconciling the right of discussion with the right of decision, may I say at once that I do not believe again that any time limit is necessary or desirable. However, if the Government is going to force on us a time limit, I find myself in the position of having to vote for the amendment so that a decision of at least 60 per cent of all Members present when the vote is taken will be necessary to put this rather iniquitous legislation into effect.

I wish to say in conclusion that this rather horrible example of blackmail put forward by the President of the Privy Council may have been only innocent kite flying on the parliamentary green. But I cannot help but think, knowing the hon. I of course find myself in an unusual position in this debate, Mr. Speaker, because I am perhaps the only Member present who knows with certainty that he will not be back. Therefore I am looking at this debate and the suggested revisions of this rule from a perspective most hon. Members cannot have. Although I tend to be somewhat combative at the moment, Mr. Speaker, it is because I seem to be encouraged to be that way by my hon. friends opposite. I can see this thing from a slightly different perspective. I know that as I will soon be returning to the life of a private citizen I will want to spend a good deal of my time listening to and endeavouring to secure the greatest possible understanding of the debates that take place on the floor of this House. Having been here it will be impossible to try to separate myself from an interest in what this House does and how it functions. There are bound to be issues develop over the next few years, as issues have developed over recent years, and it will be most important to me and to every other private citizen in the community that searching debate should take place when a genuine conflict of views develops between the Government and the Opposition.
It would be very unsatisfactory to me and to any private citizen that debate should be choked off just at a time when the public was beginning really to appreciate the inadequacy in the presentations of the Government. The only means by which I or any other private citizen could find it possible to understand what was happening in this place and what the implications of legislation were would be by the House having a debate that went on long enough to be thoroughly assessed, fully reported and then completely understood.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER WRITTEN QUESTIONS

speechtext:
How
can we fulfil our functions as an Opposition if we sit quietly by and say that this is fine, that we have nothing to say anyway? No member of this House would agree to this, No Member on the Government side would condone it either. I once sat on the Government side of the House. I now sit on the Opposition side, but I would warn hon. Members opposite that they too may find their positions reversed in due course. They must
June 7, 1965

House of Commons Procedures remember the situation they will find themselves in if they have not the right to speak, that is, if they succeed in being re-elected to this House.
I submit there must be some safeguards for the Opposition, some understanding of the total implications of this resolution upon our rules. We on this side of the House have to be satisfied in this respect. Yet the man leading the debate for the Government says, by implication, that by bringing in amendments and examining this resolution we are doing something not within the rules as Members of the Opposition. This seems to engender laughter on the other side of the House. If Government Members find it amusing then perhaps in due course they will find it necessary to answer for their amusement and lack of comprehension to the final arbiters of the positions of us all, namely, the people of Canada.
There is another side of the case which should be examined. There are many hon. Members in this House, and I am one of them, who in the years they have been here have not presumed too greatly on either the time or the temper of the House but have spoken only when they felt they must participate in debate. Many Members on this side of the House have exercised personal discipline over themselves and have willingly stayed out of debates or not sought participation in debates because they felt that their colleagues were expressing the case for their party or for themselves as well as they could. A Member who tends toward this practice is likely to find that when major debates come up he is not considered one of the star performers, not one of the Members first called upon to speak, and thus he finds it difficult to secure the floor.
This is important because there may well come a time when a Member who has deliberately chosen not to participate in every debate and talk on every subject suddenly finds, as an individual member of the House, that he is confronted with the necessity to speak if he is to fulfil his function here. But if the time for debate is limited in the way suggested by the Government in its proposal, then he will probably never get the floor. First of all will come the leaders of the parties, which of course is proper, and then the various recognized experts on the subject, as is also proper. But as it is equally proper and necessary when the backbencher suddenly finds his own interest, either political or personal, involved, that he have the right

of access to the floor in order to express the position which he feels he has been sent here to express. Consequently, by a limited debate you garrote the very man whom every party needs most, the man who occupies the backbench, because there is no Government without a very substantial backbench and there is no backbench if you deny to such Members the right to speak in this place on matters of the greatest consequence to them and their constituents.
I cannot approach this question with pretentions to being an expert on the rules of this place and I do not do so. I simply suggest to every hon. Member here that it is of some consequence to each of us as individuals, not as members of one political group or another. It is of substantial consequence to us as individual members to understand what, by acting on paragraph (6) unamended, we may be doing not only to ourselves but to all hon. Members who ever sit in this House.

maintopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER WRITTEN QUESTIONS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the Members of this House who does not feel impelled to rise in his place on every issue that comes before the House I should like to express a few thoughts on this particular measure. I have sat here for the past number of years watching the proceedings of the House and have developed a substantial respect for the institutions of Parliament and the methods by which the business of this House is conducted. I should like to be assured that the institutions which we have known will continue to function to the benefit of this country.
I sometimes wonder what sort of motivation compelled the Government to bring in these proposals at the particular time they did and in the particular manner they have. I cannot help but wonder whether this was not the result of another one of the surveys they conducted throughout the country in which they discovered, as most hon. Members of the House realize, that the Canadian people have become somewhat impatient and dissatisfied with Parliament. I suppose they felt as they felt when they took the survey on the nuclear issue in 1963, that this would be a splendid issue on which to go to the country. They know that public opinion in general is desirous of achieving some degree of efficiency in this place while at the same time not fully understanding the real purpose of Parliament and without really fully understanding why Parliament exists in the first place. I think perhaps at this time it might be well to quote from an editorial that appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of May
June 7, 1965

12, 1964, which in my opinion puts into proper perspective some of the views held by various people about Parliament. The editorial states:
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Prime Minister Pearson has referred to the "negative criticism in Canada today about the decline of our parliamentary institutions." Mr. Pearson did well to challenge this negative criticism. It's a pity that he did not single out where most of this criticism is coming from.
In his trenchant way. Sir Winston Churchill commented that the democratic system of government was the worst that could be imagined-except all other systems. Some of the commentators who leer out of TV sets these days and complain about "political partisanship" and "time wasting" in Parliament seem to have lost sight of this important fact of political life. So have the pundits who pompously complain that the present session has passed few pieces of legislation.
These commentators and pundits are frankly bored by proceedings in the House of Commons. They demand less talk and more action to liven things up. They want MPs to cease what they call "partisan bickering" and get on with the "essential business" of the country.
This attitude seems to be based on queer notions. In the first place, proceedings in Parliament were never intended to entertain those perched in the galleries around the Commons chamber. There is nothing in the Bill of Rights or the constitution that says MPs are obliged to amuse those who saunter in and out of the spectators' galleries. Nor is there any obligation to keep Hansard reporters and other recording artists in stitches.
Members of Parliament are in Ottawa for one main purpose-to talk and to express their opinions. This is the essence of the parliamentary system.
What the commentators sneeringly refer to as "partisan bickering" is the stuff of which the democratic process is made. MPs are in Ottawa to debate public questions. If Canadian voters wanted to abolish partisan bickering, they could do so by electing MPs of one political party. This would give us a one-party state without political bickering and also without political freedom. But a majority of Canadians would rather not live in a facist state even though it might result in less "time-wasting" in the Commons.
This does not mean that MPs should not be criticized on specific issues. This kind of criticism is also an essential part of the democratic process. Nor does it mean that the rules of procedure should not be streamlined to enable Parliament to deal more efficiently with the many issues that arise in the modern state.
But the sweeping, carping complaints directed at Parliament in recent months cannot be classed as constructive. Much of this criticism is not directed at the shortcomings of the government or of the opposition or of individual MPs. It comes dangerously near to being directed at the institution of Parliament itself. The danger of this kind of criticism is that it may cause some people to forget Sir Winston's admonition-the parliamentary system is the worst kind of government, except all others.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, how this attitude has developed in the minds of Canadians and why suddenly, since this Government
House of Commons Procedures assumed power, the institution of Parliament itself has become the subject of criticism. I think there is a very simple answer to this question. The Government has floundered because of an incapability to manage the affairs of the country, much less the business of this House. It has sought a whipping boy to take the blame for its inability to carry out the business of this country efficiently. There has been a need for something at which to direct criticism and the Government has selected this parliamentary institution.
Of course, the members of the press gallery who record the events of this place have become bored with various debates as they have progressed, and a prime example of this is their attitude as reflected in the press during the flag debate. I suppose in many cases many of them had to dig elsewhere for stories than this House and that laborious task tended to make them critical of this institution.
It. is a very dangerous state of affairs when we find Canadians throughout the country levelling criticisms at this democratic institution which follows the parliamentary process, as well as the Government. Very often we hear even in this place comments about partisan bickering and politics being played in the House. I am led to believe that some people want to take politics out of politics. I am not one of those who are afraid of so-called partisan bickering in the House of Commons because, as the editorial I quoted points out, this is the essence of Parliament. I am not suggesting that there cannot be an attitude of responsibility on the part, of the Members of this place and I do not mean that criticism must always be carried to dangerous extremes, but, I do suggest that when an important issue is before this place there should be no limitation on the length of time that Members of Opposition parties should take to debate a measure.
In a sense, Mr. Speaker, politicians are gladiators equipped with words as weapons. That is the only weapon a politician is equipped with to fight something he sincerely opposes. If that weapon is to be removed the Members of the Opposition will become nothing more than rubber stamps. If time limits are successfully placed on debates, then all the Government will be required to do, even when introducing unpopular legislation, is to wait out the storm.
Earlier this evening my friend, the hon. Member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh), pointed out what might have happened during
June 7, 1965

House of Commons Procedures the first stages of the Canada pension legislation had a time limit been in effect at that time. There are many other examples of legislation introduced by the Government which, if debate had been limited, might have gone through in their original state but which the Government had to amend or withdraw. This has been a general benefit to Canada and it seems to me that this is the way the situation should be.
There appears to be an attitude on the part of Government, as indicated by the speeches of hon. Members on that side of the House, that it is essential to get out of this place at the earliest possible moment, in the shortest possible time, in order to return to constituencies. I do not know about the position of most Members in this regard but I am well aware that my constituents would ask me were I to adopt that attitude: What is the great rush to get away from Ottawa? You are being paid to be there and if it takes a long time to carry out the business of Parliament effectively and efficiently, then by all means stay there.
I do not think for one moment that the people of Canada are concerned in any way if a measure requires one, two or three weeks to debate so long as the debate produces results beneficial to the nation as a whole. I have often read editorials appearing in responsible newspapers which have suggested that the Government of Canada in view of the fact that it is the biggest in this nation, ought to be run like an efficient business. Well, Mr. Speaker, this would effectively eliminate the Opposition. The board of directors' approach to Parliament would simply mean that Canadians would not be represented, the feelings of Canadians would not be taken into consideration and the effects of legislation passed in this House would be given no consideration. It would mean that we would have a totalitarian form of Government.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Surely the criterion for an effective Parliament is not simply greater efficiency. If greater efficiency is all we seek in this place, then surely we can take an example from the Russians and their form of Government because it is without a doubt the most efficient form of Government in the world. It seems to me that a democratic Government carries with it a far greater responsibility and far greater implications. It seems to me that the purpose of this place is to criticize when we feel that criticism is necessary, to oppose

when we feel opposition is beneficial and, yes, filibuster-I will even use that word-if it becomes necessary. As I said earlier, the only weapon a politician has is the weapon of words.
I heard some comment made to the effect that a time limit on debate would eliminate a lot of stupid speeches. I would not want to suggest it because 1 am afraid it would preclude a great many Members on the opposite side of the House from speaking. A time limit placed on debate would have far more serious consequencies because it would prevent the varied expressions of opinion that come from Members in this House. I have a feeling that regardless of how stupid a speech may be characterized or how silly the remarks may be, surely those remarks reflect the opinion of some Canadians somewhere in this country. If they reflect the opinion of even one Canadian, it means we have lessened his tendency toward subversive activity because then he can say that somebody in this place is saying the things he wants to hear, regardless of what they mean.

My hon. friend suggests even the hon. Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) must have some supporters for the speeches he makes in this House. I am willing to admit that this is a possibility.
The question of a time limit on debate has been mentioned earlier but I think it is worth dealing with again. We have had a perfect example during the Wednesday question period of what would happen if there was a time limit. It seems to me that the Government saves up for that particular day all the questions they have been unable to answer during the course of the week and then comes into the House armed with lengthy replies to questions and takes up all the time thus preventing Members of the House from asking further questions. I am not afraid of a limit on the question period provided there is one day a week in which there is no limit on the time for the question period. I believe that Wednesday, which is a short day, would be a fairly good day to allow the question period to run right through to five o'clock, private Members' hour.
We are somewhat concerned about the attitude that this Government has taken over certain measures. I want to refer to comments that were made by Members of the Government during the twenty fourth Parliament when we had a rather large number
June 7, 1965

of Members on the other side of the House and we were the Government. I recall the oft-repeated statement made by Liberal campaigners during the 1962 election to the effect that if they had 208 Members on that side of the House they could do anything; they could pass any amount of legislation. Might is right in their opinion. It is this attitude, this state of mind, on the part of the Liberals that causes me to worry about their intentions on this particular issue. Heaven help us if they ever get a sufficient majority that would enable them to carry through legislation. Their attitude seems to be that if they can carry it all they have to do is hide behind the rule they are proposing to make now and wait out the storm and they will be able to pass any legislation in this Parliament.
We have seen something of their attitude, Mr. Speaker. I saw it in the flag debate. We hear talk about a republic from some hon. Members opposite. We have noted their recent move in respect of the Coat of Arms of Canada, the constant sniping at our established institutions and the statements and resolutions passed by the young Liberals of this country. All of these things cause us to wonder what is the motivation behind this proposed change. To be quite frank with you, Mr. Speaker, I suspect their motives. If their past actions are any indication of what they propose to do, then we have every cause in the world to be alarmed and we most certainly have every justification for opposing this legislation for all we are worth.

Mr. Speaker, in rising at this time to join this debate may I say I did not want to deprive the House of the sort of perspective one can get when one comes from a part of Canada that has not really been wholeheartedly accepted into Canada or the Canadian Parliament by southern Canadians. Those of us who live in my part of the country often feel that the attitude of the people who live in the south is to treat us as if we were a sort of senile aunt living in an upstairs attic, an attic that is cold and drafty and, when necessary, you will invite us down to have a meal but never when there are important people visiting. I have no better example of this attitude than the Prime Minister's (Mr. Pearson) answer today that the Governments of the Yukon and Northwest Territories are not to participate on a consultation basis in the discussions that are going on in relation to designated areas but rather he is 22620-133
House of Commons Procedures going to tell us what he and the ten provincial Premiers have decided once they have decided. I say this by way of introduction knowing it will only set the tone for my remarks as a resident of Canada's far north, not because I think it particularly pertinent to the item before the House, e (9:10 p.m.)
The question of rule changes contains a basic problem. It is not the changes in themselves though even these may contain dangers for Members, particularly backbenchers. The basic danger is that those of us who sit in Opposition quite frankly do not trust the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcll-raith) or any other members of the millionaire Cabinet who are about to introduce these changes. I am not suggesting for one second that the President of the Privy Council is himself a millionaire. I realize this requires certain circumstances of birth, fortune and ability that perhaps exclude him. None the less, quite frankly we are not afraid of the rules. We are afraid of the Government Members who sit on the front benches and the way they are likely to apply the rules.
In my short term in this chamber the only thing I can go by is the way the treasury benches approach the business of the House of Commons. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and all other hon. Members, that these people intend to use this limitation rule in both the biblical sense of the word "use" and in the worst sense of that word, which means to suit their own purposes. I have seen what happens when a Government such as the one we have today, which is populated with what I call the intellectual Fascists of Canada, decides what is good for people. Intellectual Fascists I am prepared to define as all those people who believe that unless you are a Rhodes scholar or have been an assistant deputy minister at some stage in your career -Lord knows, the treasury benches are full of both those categories-you do not really know what is good for people.
There is no better example than the special adviser who has been hired to work in the office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). He, without a doubt in my mind, is the one who is promoting these changes in the rules. I am referring to Mr. Kent, that $26,000 a year co-ordinator, the new director of the war on poverty, the man who takes over when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) cannot handle the Quebec situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider the matter now before the House one of the most important to be discussed here in many years. I would not be at all surprised to hear groans from the other side and demands of "Question". I say this because apparently hon. Members on the other side do not seem to realize that the measure we are now dealing with is of extreme importance. In my opinion it might determine to a large extent the function and the role of this House as part of the Parliament of Canada in the years to come.
The first part of the resolution is, of course, not contentious. It provides for a limitation of the time which is to be spent on estimates, the time being 30 days, and for six supply motions be replaced by four. This part of the proposal, Mr. Speaker, is quite different from the original proposal of the Government. The change that has occurred in this
June 7, 1965

House of Commons Procedures part of the motion indicates what can be done when the Government genuinely considers changes and modifications which are suggested by the Opposition.
Here I should like to make a comment, as did the hon. Member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume), regarding the press gallery and particularly the press media of Canada. I believe they have been most unfair in reporting the general attitude of the Official Opposition toward the changes proposed in the rules of this House by the Government. The first speech made on behalf of the Official Opposition was th_c of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) on May 20. I listened very carefully to that speech and to me the gist of it was that the proposals made by the Government did not go far enough, that reform of the procedures of this House was necessary but that the measures proposed by the Government were not effective. This was the general impression created on me by the speech of the Leader of the Opposition. The next day the news indicated in effect that the Official Opposition were opposing the proposed reforms of the House. This line taken by the news media follows upon careful and clever preparation by the Liberal party in advance of introducing these reforms.
The Government is aware of the fact, as are we, that at this time the Parliament of Canada is held in rather low repute by the people of Canada. The people consider that it is necessary for the House to become more effective and that therefore changes to make it more effective are necessary. The Government is making use of this general attitude of the people in trying to push through reforms, some of which are not good. Probably 90 per cent or more of the reforms proposed by the Government, Mr. Speaker, are acceptable to us. Most of them would be even more acceptable were the major reform proposed by the Leader of the Opposition of the establishment of a permanent Speaker agreed to by the Government. In that event many of the proposals of the Government would become more acceptable to us.
The second part of the motion concerns what is commonly referred to as the guillotine proposal. Briefly, it provides that a Business Committee shall be set up with one Member to be selected by each party of the House. This Business Committee shall allocate time for any item of legislation or business to be brought before the House.

If the recommendation of this Committee is not unanimous, then a Minister may introduce a motion to limit time which is debatable for one day. This motion would put a limit on the debate of the particular item of business of not less than five days made up of two days for second reading, two days for the Committee stage and one day for third reading. This motion could also restrict the time of the speeches of Members of this House.
I might say that I think it would be most necessary, in view of such allocation of the time of individual speakers, to make special allowance for the length of the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Opposition, both of whom are officers of the House, and for the Minister who introduces the particular item of business and the Member of the Opposition who replies thereto.
As the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) has pointed out, a two-day debate with a limitation of 20 minutes per speaker would allow only 42 Members of the House to speak. If a five-day limitation were applied only some 100 Members of the House, assuming no Member spoke twice at a different stage of the debate, would be allowed to speak on the question. Thus 160 Members would be silenced.
As a backbencher I will be one of those 160. Many Members on the other side, particularly the backbenchers, will be included in those who will be silenced. Last week three or four Liberal backbenchers spoke of their concern for the rights of the backbenchers. I think they should consider the situation where some 160 Members of this House could be silenced by the introduction of the guillotine.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The amendment moved by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) is to the effect that the motion introduced by the Minister to allocate time and apply the guillotine shall not be effected unless 60 per cent of the Members present in the House approve of such motion. I think I can claim credit for being the author of this idea. So far as I know, I was the first to suggest it to this side of the House.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) objected on Friday on the grounds that this would be in contravention of Section 49 of the British North America Act
June 7, 1965	COMMONS
because the proposed amendment suggests that any decision of the House of Commons in regard to limitation be based on a vote of at least 60 per cent of the Members present and the B.N.A. Act states that any decision of the House of Commons must be made on a majority basis.
I have looked up the Oxford dictionary definition of "majority" which states that "majority" means the greater number, more than half of certain people or things, number of votes cast for the other side or any opponent. I am a complete layman when it comes to an interpretation of legislation, but it seems to me that with a will on the part of the Government the provisions of section
49	of the B.N.A. Act could well be interpreted to mean that the majority is any number more than one half of the individuals present. It is interesting to note that if in fact the President of the Privy Council is correct the House today could decide by a so-called majority, which is one more than
50	per cent, that tomorrow the vote in this regard will be based on a 60 per cent majority.
This situation reminds me of the story about a convention of learned professors who were trying to decide whether the majority is always right or is sometimes wrong. They held a vote on the question and a majority of the professors decided that the majority was always wrong. I repeat that if there is a will on the part of the Government to get around this contentious proposal to implement the guillotine measure there is a way.
I note in today's Toronto Star that the President of the Privy Council is reported as having indicated that unless we buckle under to the Government's proposal there will be an election. That of course confirms the allegation by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) on May 20 when he referred to the same type of threat by the Government, at which time the President of the Privy Council denied any such intent to call an election if we did not go along with the Government's proposal.
The President of the Privy Council is now in his seat and I hope he will give attention to the suggestion I now intend to make. I have in mind his statement as recorded in the Toronto Star and I should like to outline some amendments I have in mind. Rather than take up the time of the House by proposing these amendments, I would ask the Minister to consider these ideas, namely, that the motion to be made by a Minister for the allocation of time shall not become

House of Commons Procedures effective or applicable unless the subject matter of business under consideration has been referred to a special or standing committee of the House and not until such committee has reported. I hope the President of the Privy Council will give this suggestion some consideration because, although I am not speaking as a spokesman for our party, if it would be acceptable as an amendment by the Government it does seem to me it would meet some of the objections posed by hon. Members in the Opposition.
If there is to be any allocation of time such an allocation would be more acceptable and justifiable if it was invoked after a committee had considered the question and reported.

AIR TRANSPORT-CANADIAN PACIFIC AIRLINES-ASSURANCE RESPECTING ASSIGNED AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) announced the installation of a new national air policy with regard to international flights by Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines. At that time the air critic for the New Democratic Party, the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie), commented on the Minister's statement. As a result of those comments I asked the question which I am now debating on the late show.
Air Canada, as I think most Members of this House will agree, is one of the world's great national air lines of which we as Canadians are justly proud. I think the management and staff can be equally as proud of the services that air line provides Canadians.
Under the new policy Air Canada will be protected and preserved in its international flights. One of the remarkable things about the new policy, and one which I as a resident of British Columbia am so happy to see, is that the Canadian Pacific Airlines, with its headquarters in Vancouver, will also be protected and preserved in its international flights.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
It has seemed to some of us over the years that Government policy has been designed with the idea that Canadian Pacific Airlines has been something of an unwanted child in Canadian aviation. This Government and the Minister of Transport have now recognized the importance of Canadian Pacific Airlines in Canadian aviation. It has guaranteed the continued existence, future development and growth of this Canadian air line. It has also,
[Mr. Chatterton.l
by preserving its flights and appointing Canadian Pacific Airlines a chosen instrument of the Government in Latin America, Asia, the Pacific area and Southern Europe, assured that the international airport of the City of Vancouver will become the second air capital of Canada and will become the crossroads of trans-Pacific and Latin American travel.
It is this importance of Canadian Pacific Airlines to Vancouver and British Columbia which caused me to be shocked and surprised by the remarks of the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie). Canadian Pacific employs some 1,900 people in British Columbia, about 1,850 of them in the Vancouver area, and I daresay a large proportion of them in Burnaby-Richmond itself. They receive in salaries and wages some $12 million per year and most of it is spent in the Vancouver area. I am sure a large proportion of it is spent in Burnaby-Richmond. Another $11 million is pumped into the Province's economy in purchases of goods and services. The C.P.A. purchasing staff does business with some 700 suppliers in British Columbia, many of them I am sure located in Burnaby-Richmond. For example, only recently after a year and a half of development and exploration a British Columbia firm was able to develop the mobile passenger stairway that they use in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Edmonton and Montreal. Formerly these were imported from the United States but because of the initiative of Canadian Pacific Airlines they are now made in British Columbia.
It is because of this importance of Canadian Pacific Airlines to British Columbia that I was shocked when the Member for Burnaby-Richmond expressed these comments to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), as reported on page 1816 of Hansard:
At first glance it seems to me the division of the world is not quite equal and that C.P.A. has a much greater territory than Air Canada.
Certainly the implication of the N.D.P. critic's statement was that the Canadian Government was being too kind to Canadian Pacific Airlines, that Canadian Pacific Airlines were being treated too well by this Government. This implication coming from a Member of the N.D.P. is quite understandable. This party, being a socialist party, has no sympathy for the privately owned Canadian Pacific Airlines. They would, I am sure, favour the amalgamation or the merger of the Canadian Pacific Airlines with Air Can-
June 7, 1965

ada into one nationalized Government owned air line.
This policy, Mr. Speaker, would be disastrous for British Columbia. It would automatically result in the centralization of all air activities in the City of Montreal. Vancouver would be placed in the same position as Winnipeg now is whereby economic factors must force the centralization of purchasing and servicing in one centre. By the continued existence of Canadian Pacific Airlines and by its protection under this new air policy, Vancouver will retain its position and its importance in the field of international air travel.
I am shocked that a company that is so important to the riding of Burnaby-Richmond should be downgraded in this way by a Member who represents that area in the House of Commons.
This policy of the N.D.P., like most policies of the N.D.P., would do nothing but cost British Columbians their jobs and incomes. Hence my question last Wednesday to the Minister of Transport, wanting his assurance that the agreement that has been worked out with the presidents of C.P.A. and Air Canada will be adhered to, that the allocations of the areas of the world given to each will be adhered to and that he will not listen, as I am confident he will not, to the entreaties of the N.D.P., the socialist party of Canada, to derogate from the position of C.P.A.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate arises out of a question which was first put by the hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) on June 1 and followed up by myself on June 3 and 4. On June 1, as recorded at page 1820 of Hansard, the hon. Member for Kootenay West said:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Labour. Can the Minister of Labour explain to the House why at this date that runaway criminal, Harold Chamberlain Banks, is still President of the Canadian Seafarers Building Corporation Limited, a private company which controls all properties owned by the Seafarers International Union in Canada?
To which the Minister answered:
No, Mr. Speaker, I cannot explain something which I do not believe is correct.
I suggest that when the Minister gave that answer he had not even asked his staff to look into the situation, feeling that if he gave that kind of glib answer he would get away with it and nothing would be heard about the matter again. But on June 3 and 4 I pressed the matter again. I asked if this was correct and, if it was not correct, what were the facts.
The Minister's answer to these questions whether Banks is still president of the Seafarers Building Corporation Limited was that he would look into the matter. Finally that is what he said. For several days he went on looking into the matter, when all it would take was three or four minutes to call up the Department of the Secretary of State, the Companies Branch, and find out if the facts were correct, which I did. I found that not only was Mr. Banks president of that corporation but that Mr. McLaughlin was a director.
Let us just look at this situation for a few moments. First of all, the Minister was very evasive. I said the other day, and I got myself into some difficulty, that either the Minister had deliberately misled the House or he had given a careless answer. It had to be one or the other, and I would say at the very least it was certainly a careless answer.
Of course, one runs into this difficulty under the rules of the House that if a Minister
June 7, 1965
2084	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion or Member says something is the fact you cannot question his word under the rules, but that does not say that still down in your heart you do not feel the situation is wrong. You cannot legislate your feelings.
Let us take a look at the situation so far as the Norris Report is concerned, even for the short time that Mr. McLaughlin is substituting for Mr. Banks in this enterprise. It is rather a shocking situation, and the point I want to make first is that when we had the trustees before the Industrial Relations Committee we got nowhere. They refused to answer the questions properly. Questions were put suggesting that the election which resulted in Mr. McLaughlin becoming president of the S.I.U. was not a properly conducted democratic election. They were never answered. Mr. Justice Dryer, called before the committee, only stayed a few hours one day before leaving in a huff for British Columbia saying he would not come back unless he was subpoenaed. We on this side have continually urged that the trustees should be brought back before the committee to give these answers. The question I should like to ask now is this: Why have the three trustees not been brought before that committee?
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The Chairman of the committee, a man for whom I have great respect and a friend of mine, gave great consideration to points of order and questions of privilege, so that in the end we got no information. The trustees might just as well not have appeared before the committee. The whole thing was a sham. Why are the Government and the Liberal party hiding the facts? What skeletons are in the closet that they should have to hide these facts? We have continually been given evasive answers with reference to Banks' escape-

speechtext:
Don't worry about the rules. You would like to gag Parliament so that this information would never be given to the Canadian people. That is why you want to change the rules. Mr. Justice Norris said:
McLaughlin has proved his usefulness to Banks at headquarters meetings. He is devious and adept in carrying out the one-man policies of Banks and in assisting in setting up the farce of democracy in the union.
In other words, he was a henchman of Banks. Why is it that the trustees did nothing to explain to the committee why he became the President of the union? Mr. Banks' hench-


man, Mr. Banks' agent, is still running this corporation. Banks is running it through McLaughlin. These are the facts and they cannot be hidden by the Minister of Labour.
What else did Mr. Justice Norris say? This is what he said as reported at page 307:
The Trusteeship Act should contain a provision that any transfer of union assets, real or personal after the date of this Report and until the trustees have taken office, shall be void save the expenditure of such sums of money as the trustees shall certify have been reasonable and proper on union business.
The assets should have been taken over from a man such as Banks who has fled the law and gone to the United States and from a man such as McLaughlin who, we maintained in the committee, was never democratically elected as President of the S.I.U. The Government has been most evasive so far as the S.I.U. and the trustees are concerned. We say this. First, let us get the trustees before the committee. If you have nothing to hide, bring them before the committee and let the Opposition ask those searching questions so that the Canadian public and the members of the S.I.U. may know the facts and so that their representations can be placed properly before Parliament. Further, let the committee be under the Chairmanship of a man who will allow us to ask these questions instead of permitting so many points of order and questions of privilege and adjourning this and that with the result that we never got the facts from the witnesses, that is to say, the trustees. I say the record speaks for itself in this regard.

A committee is bound by, and is not at liberty to depart from, the order of reference.

Mr. Speaker, the situation with respect to the committee meeting is that when the procedural resolution is dealt with, we hope to set up the committee. Presumably the estimates of the Department of Labour could then be sent to the appropriate committee, which would provide an opportunity for Members to deal with any aspect of the operations of the Department-
I underline these words, Mr. Speaker:
-including the item with respect to the maritime trustees. That would seem to be the efficient way to meet the point made by my hon. friend.
After hearing the officers of the Department of Labour and the Minister of Labour, should it be deemed necessary and the House feels there is more information it wishes to obtain, I am sure the Government would be glad to put the matter before the House to determine whether the House wishes to have the trustees brought before that committee again. It should be a determination of the House and can only be done by a determination of the House.

speechtext:
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion these things should be included in our automobiles is no easy task.
I know that the Minister or whoever is going to speak on his behalf will agree with what I have said about the importance of this matter and that there are some devices which have been proven to be useful in this area but, of course, the reply will be that this is a matter which comes under provincial jurisdiction. I make the plea, Mr. Speaker, that instead of putting energy into finding excuses for not acting in this field the Government ought to put energy into finding ways in which it can act.
I remember in this House when Mr. Speaker Glen-I am going back a few years-ruled out of order any discussion on the floor of the House about the question of a Trans-Canada Highway because highways came under provincial jurisdiction. But in due course a way was found to pass the Trans-Canada Highway Act in this Parliament. Hospitalization is a provincial matter, but we found a way in which to bring in legislation at the federal field, under which we now have hospitalization across the country. Medicare is regarded as a provincial matter, but all parties recognize that the day is coming when we will have federal legislation in this field. And so I could go on down the list. There are all kinds of things thought to come under provincial jurisdiction but concerning which, when the interests of the nation are at stake, a way can be found to deal with them at the federal level.
The right is set out in the British North America Act to declare certain works to be to the general advantage of Canada. Surely because automobiles are manufactured in only two or three provinces we should not leave it to the governments of those provinces to deal with this matter. Surely this is a matter of concern to the people of Canada from coast to coast and the Government should take a lead in it.
I would be satisfied if the Government took positive action to get the provinces to act in the matter but we see no sign of this. I suggest that the time has come for the federal Government to realize that it is the Government which has to speak for Canadians from coast to coast. Cars travel everywhere. Death is taking place on our highways in all provinces. It can be prevented by action. The people of Canada call for this kind of action. I put to the Government the straightforward question: Instead of finding ways and means to avoid action, why not put some energy

into finding a way in which the federal Government can act so that we can have safer automobiles than we have at the present time, and thus cut down the awful death toll that takes place on our highways?

These provincial statutes and regulations pertain both to physical characteristics involving safety and the manner in which the vehicle is operated.
It is recognized that a great deal of work has been undertaken by various bodies to determine the areas where improvement in design or vehicle construction can lead to greater safety. Thus, a great deal of good research and information respecting safety has been developed. This information would be useful in preparing a safety code.
